claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by interface-mediated dislocation behavior modulated by short-range order.
Dislocations interact with compositional complexity and short-range ordering at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interfacial compositional complexity and short-range order control dislocation mobility and accumulation.
Changes in dislocation mobility and accumulation determine the creep deformation rate.
The starting multilayers possess inherent lattice distortion.
The starting multilayers have observable short-range order at their interfaces.
Sustained loading generates dislocations in each layer that encounter FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interfacial short-range order acts as a pinning or modifying site for dislocation motion.
Pinning or modification of dislocation motion causes interfacial dislocation accumulation or pile-up.
Altered dislocation mobility, rather than enhanced diffusion or mobility arising solely from lattice distortion, controls the creep rate.
Greater interfacial short-range order will produce a lower creep rate through increased dislocation pinning.
Greater interfacial short-range order will produce a distinct pattern of interfacial dislocation accumulation.
Conventional multilayers used as a baseline lack the compositional complexity of the proposed high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
The proposed mechanism applies to multilayers with layer thicknesses below approximately 100 nm.
The proposed mechanism applies in temperature and stress regimes that activate thermally assisted dislocation motion without causing catastrophic interface failure or coalescence.
